### Problem: Minimum cost for tickets {#sec-od-p1-tickets}

::: {.p-statement}
You travel on the days in `days` (strictly increasing, each day between 1 and 365). A 1-day pass costs `costs[0]`, a 7-day pass costs `costs[1]`, and a 30-day pass costs `costs[2]`. A pass covers that many consecutive days starting on the day you buy it. Return the minimum cost of being able to travel on every day in `days`.

$1 \le n \le 365$, and each cost is between 1 and 1000. On days $[1,4,6,7,8,20]$ with costs $[2,7,15]$ the answer is 11. On days $1..10, 30, 31$ with the same costs the answer is 17.

Source: [LC 983 · Minimum Cost For Tickets](https://leetcode.com/problems/minimum-cost-for-tickets/){.solved difficulty="Medium"}
:::

::: {.p-intuition}
Look at the last travel day $d$ of a prefix. Some pass covers it. Slide that pass so that it ends on day $d$: it still covers $d$, and it still covers every earlier travel day it covered before. What remains is the same problem on the travel days up to day $d - D$. Three pass lengths, three smaller calendars. Buying the week on the first busy day is greedy, and it loses: on days $[13,16,18,19,21,22]$ with costs $[2,7,15]$ that rule spends 11, and the optimum spends 9 by leaving day 13 on a 1-day pass and starting the week on day 16.
:::

::: {.p-approach}
- **State (day).** $dp[d]$ = minimum cost to cover every travel day at most $d$.
- **Transition (day).** A quiet day copies $dp[d-1]$. A travel day takes $\min\big(dp[d-1]+c_1,\ dp[\max(0,d-7)]+c_7,\ dp[\max(0,d-30)]+c_{30}\big)$.
- **State (event).** $E[i]$ = minimum cost to cover the first $i$ trips.
- **Transition (event).** A pass of length $D$ ending on day $d = \mathrm{days}[i-1]$ looks back to the first trip with day $> d - D$.
- **Base.** $dp[0] = E[0] = 0$. **Answer.** $dp[\mathrm{last}] = E[n]$. **Order.** Increasing $d$, or increasing $i$.
:::

::: {.callout-important title="Why the travel-day pointers match the day table"}
Between trips the day table is constant, so the value on trip $i$ equals $E[i]$. A 7-day pass that ends on day $d$ covers days $d-6..d$. The trips it leaves behind are exactly those with day $\le d-7$, and $dp[d-7]$ is the cost after the last of them. That is $E[j_7]$.

The same index only moves forward as $d$ grows, so each pointer walks the trip list once. Clamping a day-index at 0 is the same fact: a pass bought on day 1 reaches back to the empty start. The two tables therefore store the same numbers, the day table in many repeated copies. Count the states. A calendar of 365 days wants the day table. Coordinates up to $10^9$, or many pass lengths, want the pointers.
:::

The buttons are in order. Each one keeps the previous solution and changes only what that form changes.

::: {.panel-tabset .solution-forms}

#### Recursion

::: {.form-next}
`f(i)` is the minimum cost of trips `i` through the end. The pass that covers trip `i` can start on `days[i]`. Try lengths 1, 7, and 30. Each pass jumps to the first trip whose day is at least `days[i] + length`. Those three groups of plans are disjoint and cover every plan, so the costs take a minimum. `f(n) = 0`: nothing left to cover. The answer is `f(0)`.
:::

```{python}

#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    title, inp, steps, final = Traces.get("tickets", "rec")
    assert str(final) == "11"
    V.story(ax, p, title, inp, steps, final)
V.show(draw)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
#| label: od-tickets-rec
def tickets_rec(days, costs):
    n, dur = len(days), (1, 7, 30)

    def f(i):
        if i >= n:
            return 0
        best = 10**18
        for p in range(3):
            j = i
            while j < n and days[j] < days[i] + dur[p]:
                j += 1
            best = min(best, costs[p] + f(j))
        return best

    return f(0)
```

##### C++

```cpp
int ticketsRec(int i, const vector<int>& days, const vector<int>& costs) {
    int n = days.size();
    if (i >= n) return 0;
    int dur[3] = {1, 7, 30};
    int best = 2000000000;
    for (int p = 0; p < 3; ++p) {
        int j = i;
        while (j < n && days[j] < days[i] + dur[p]) ++j;
        best = min(best, costs[p] + ticketsRec(j, days, costs));
    }
    return best;
}
```
:::

#### Memo

::: {.form-next}
The recursion is the right answer, and it recomputes it. There are `n + 1` distinct calls. `memo[i]` is filled the first time `f(i)` returns and read after that. The body is the previous button; the array in front of the recursive calls is the new line.
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    title, inp, steps, final = Traces.get("tickets", "memo")
    assert str(final) == "11"
    V.story(ax, p, title, inp, steps, final)
V.show(draw)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
def tickets_memo(days, costs):
    n, dur = len(days), (1, 7, 30)
    memo = [None] * (n + 1)

    def f(i):
        if i >= n:
            return 0
        if memo[i] is None:
            best = 10**18
            for p in range(3):
                j = i
                while j < n and days[j] < days[i] + dur[p]:
                    j += 1
                best = min(best, costs[p] + f(j))
            memo[i] = best
        return memo[i]

    return f(0)
```

##### C++

```cpp
int ticketsMemo(int i, const vector<int>& days, const vector<int>& costs, vector<int>& memo) {  // memo filled with -1
    int n = days.size();
    if (i >= n) return 0;
    if (memo[i] >= 0) return memo[i];
    int dur[3] = {1, 7, 30};
    int best = 2000000000;
    for (int p = 0; p < 3; ++p) {
        int j = i;
        while (j < n && days[j] < days[i] + dur[p]) ++j;
        best = min(best, costs[p] + ticketsMemo(j, days, costs, memo));
    }
    return memo[i] = best;
}
```
:::

#### Day table

::: {.form-next}
The year has 365 days, so give every day a cell and fill from the left. The calls go away. On a day with no travel, yesterday's cost is already the answer: copy it. On a travel day the pass can be slid to end today, so the look-back is the fixed set `d - 1`, `d - 7`, `d - 30`, and a look-back before day 0 reads `dp[0]`. The answer is `dp[last]`.
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    title, inp, steps, final = Traces.get("tickets", "day")
    assert str(final) == "11"
    V.story(ax, p, title, inp, steps, final)
V.show(draw)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
def tickets_day(days, costs):
    last = days[-1]
    travel = set(days)
    dp = [0] * (last + 1)
    for d in range(1, last + 1):
        if d not in travel:
            dp[d] = dp[d - 1]
            continue
        dp[d] = min(dp[d - 1] + costs[0],
                    dp[max(0, d - 7)] + costs[1],
                    dp[max(0, d - 30)] + costs[2])
    return dp[last]
```

##### C++

```cpp
int ticketsDay(const vector<int>& days, const vector<int>& costs) {
    int last = days.back();
    vector<char> travel(last + 1, 0);
    for (int d : days) travel[d] = 1;
    vector<int> dp(last + 1, 0);
    for (int d = 1; d <= last; ++d) {
        if (!travel[d]) { dp[d] = dp[d - 1]; continue; }
        dp[d] = min(dp[d - 1] + costs[0],
                    min(dp[max(0, d - 7)] + costs[1], dp[max(0, d - 30)] + costs[2]));
    }
    return dp[last];
}
```
:::

#### Travel days

::: {.form-next}
Quiet days are copies of the previous travel day. Keep one state per trip. `E[i]` is the cost of the first `i` trips, which is the day-table value on that trip's day. A pass of length `D` ending on day `d` excludes every trip on or before day `d - D`. As `i` grows, that index only moves right, so one pointer per duration replaces the subtraction `d - D`. For a 7-day pass the test is `days[j] <= d - 7`, because the pass covers `d - 6 .. d`.
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    title, inp, steps, final = Traces.get("tickets", "event")
    assert str(final) == "11"
    V.story(ax, p, title, inp, steps, final)
V.show(draw)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
def tickets_event(days, costs):
    n = len(days)
    E = [0] * (n + 1)
    j7 = j30 = 0
    for i in range(1, n + 1):
        d = days[i - 1]
        while days[j7] <= d - 7:
            j7 += 1
        while days[j30] <= d - 30:
            j30 += 1
        E[i] = min(E[i - 1] + costs[0], E[j7] + costs[1], E[j30] + costs[2])
    return E[n]

def _rand_days(last, n):
    return sorted(random.sample(range(1, last + 1), n))

for _ in range(25):
    last = random.randint(1, 30)
    days = _rand_days(last, random.randint(1, min(7, last)))
    costs = [random.randint(1, 15) for _ in range(3)]
    assert tickets_rec(days, costs) == tickets_memo(days, costs) == tickets_day(days, costs) == tickets_event(days, costs)
assert tickets_event([1, 4, 6, 7, 8, 20], [2, 7, 15]) == 11
assert tickets_event(list(range(1, 11)) + [30, 31], [2, 7, 15]) == 17
assert tickets_event([13, 16, 18, 19, 21, 22], [2, 7, 15]) == 9
assert tickets_event([1, 2, 3], [10, 3, 20]) == 3
assert tickets_day(list(range(1, 366)), [2, 7, 15]) == 187
```

##### C++

```cpp
int ticketsEvent(const vector<int>& days, const vector<int>& costs) {
    int n = days.size();
    vector<int> E(n + 1, 0);
    int j7 = 0, j30 = 0;
    for (int i = 1; i <= n; ++i) {
        int d = days[i - 1];
        while (days[j7] <= d - 7) ++j7;
        while (days[j30] <= d - 30) ++j30;
        E[i] = min(E[i - 1] + costs[0], min(E[j7] + costs[1], E[j30] + costs[2]));
    }
    return E[n];
}
```
:::

:::

::: {.p-complexity}
**Recursion** up to $3^n$ calls. **Memoisation** $O(n^2)$ when each state walks the trip list, or $O(n \log n)$ if each jump is a binary search. **Day table** $O(\mathrm{last}) \le 365$. **Travel days** $O(n)$: each pointer moves at most $n$ times. The day table is the short program. The pointers are the program that still works when days reach $10^9$.
:::

::: {.p-edge}
- One travel day: pay the cheapest of the three passes. With costs $[10,3,20]$ that is the 7-day pass.
- Days 1 and 365 are two isolated trips, and $d-30$ clamps at 0. The answer is 4 for costs $[2,7,15]$.
- Several optimal plans can share a cost. On the first sample, a 7-day pass on day 1 plus 1-day passes on days 8 and 20 is also 11.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistakes"}
- Filling only the travel days leaves quiet days at 0, so $dp[d-7]$ often reads a 0 and the answer comes out too small.
- Nothing says a longer pass costs more. On days $[1,2,3]$ with costs $[10,3,20]$ the answer is 3, a single 7-day pass.
- A 7-day pass ending on day $d$ covers $d-6..d$. The pointer skips trips with day $\le d-7$. A strict `<` covers a trip exactly 7 days earlier, and the first sample drops from 11 to 9.
:::

**Variants.** Several pass lengths on a calendar that reaches $10^9$ are the same event table, one pointer per length, and the day array is simply too big. A charge printed after each trip, with tickets of 1 ride, 90 minutes, and a day, is that table differenced: [CF 756B · Travel Card](https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/756/B){rating="1600"}. A purchase of fruit $i$ that makes the next $i$ fruits free is a window whose left end only moves right: [LC 2944 · Minimum Number of Coins for Fruits](https://leetcode.com/problems/minimum-number-of-coins-for-fruits/){difficulty="Medium"}. A monthly pass, valid for a calendar month, changes only the third look-back, from $d-30$ to the day before the first of the month.
